I'm writing to David Gewirtz in the text below, not Kleyno. :)

Reason #1: Honestly? The only question that went through my mind at the mention of Mint was "Why was that particular distro chosen?" People have different reasons for running different distros.

Corporations that are trying to save money will run RHEL on a handful of servers that need support if things go pear-shaped, and CentOS on everything else. Why? Because CentOS is the exact same thing as RHEL, but without the support. It's all built from the same RPMs, except for the branding.

I've used maybe a half dozen distributions in the 20+ years I've been using Linux. Each was chosen because it suited my needs at the time.

Reason #2: "For all of us who have lives"? By uttering that phrase, you became as bad as the fanbois you despise so much. Congratulations.

No system is going to go completely untouched. Servers need updates periodically. Workstations and personal systems need updates too. It doesn't matter what OS they're running.

The trick is that if one knows what one is doing, then one needn't be "hands-on" any more often than necessary. If a system needs constant attention, there's something dreadfully wrong.

Reason #3: Your video is amusing, but it is hardly typical.

Stereotypically, Windows admins are people who can't learn enough to move on to other operating systems. The truth is that most Windows admins are really very good at what they do. They know as many tricks for Windows Server as a knowledgeable Linux admin knows about their favorite distro.

At the end of the day, one simply has to use the right tool for the job.

Reason #4: If one wishes to gripe about application availability, one needs to blame the authors of the applications, not the operating system. Adobe has their reasons for not making their stuff available for Linux, mostly centering around the cost of porting the software versus the amount they'd make selling that version. (This applies to Microsoft and their Office suite as well.)

As for EverNote, it is available for Android, which is Linux under the hood. Why isn't it available for desktop Linux? Probably because the authors do not perceive the effort to be worth putting it there.

Reason #5: Define "pleasant".

Windows systems (especially desktop versions) carry a ton of baggage that comes with having to account for a million or more different hardware configurations. That is part of the reason why the BSoD happens so often.

I can drop a LiveCD on any system with a CDROM drive, boot it, and do whatever I need to do. Write a document, spreadsheet, or presentation? Done AND Microsoft Office apps will read the files. I can research papers, I can do almost anything without installing anything else.

Summary

I've said it before, I'll say it again: Use the right tool for the job.

Want to do graphic design or video editing? Use a Mac.

Want to do general work and do it efficiently and well? Use unix or Linux.

Want to play games? Use Windows.
